newsitem.title: USA: Family's lawyer presses expert in Reynolds trial.
newsitem.headline: Family's lawyer presses expert in Reynolds trial.

text.p: A pathologist called to the witness stand Monday by R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. hotly defended his testimony that smoking did not necessarily cause the lung cancer of the late Jean Connor.

Connor's family is suing Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., for allegedly manufacturing a dangerous product. Connor, who died two years ago at age 49, had been a heavy smoker of Reynolds' Salem-brand cigarettes.

During questioning by Norwood Wilner, an attorney for the Connor family, pathologist Dr. Sanford Barsky from the UCLA Medical Centre said he had seen no tissue samples or other evidence which would allow him to conclude Connor's cancer had begun in one of her lungs.
Other witnesses, including a pathologist from Duke University called by Wilner, have said they were virtually certain Connor's cancer had begun in a lung.
In often testy exchanges, during which the pathologist was instructed by the trial judge to answer Wilner's questions, Barsky said he agreed cigarette smoking was a major cause of cancer.
But, he added, statistical evidence drawn from large groups did not necessarily apply to individual cases such as Connor's.
Wilner asked Barsky if he believed smoking caused cancer.
"There probably was a causal relationship," Barsky said, but declined to say when pushed by Wilner that smoking clearly spurred the disease.
Barsky disputed very strongly Wilner's claim that the lung cancer rate among non-smokers was negligible.
Wilner asked if Barsky agreed that as much as 90 percent of lung cancer deaths would be avoided if cigarettes were unavailable.
"It's hard to say what would happen if everyone stopped smoking ... but, if you're asking if lung cancer would go away, I think not," Barsky said.
